reason: The king of Israel does demonstrate accountability in this passage, albeit reactive rather than proactive. When a woman cries out to him for help during the famine, he responds by asking what the matter is. Upon learning of the cannibalism agreement between women due to the siege, he tears his clothes (v. 30) and wears sackcloth (v. 30), demonstrating he accepts the gravity of the situation and his people's suffering. He investigates the matter by sending scouts to verify the prophet's claim about the lifting of the siege (v. 14). Additionally, his officer faces direct accountability—he is trampled to death at the gate for doubting God's word (v. 17, 20), demonstrating that skeptical leadership is held answerable. While the king's response is limited in scope and the ultimate resolution comes through divine intervention rather than his own initiative, he does take meaningful accountability by responding to the crisis and seeking to address it, rather than ignoring it entirely.
